derives_from: **There is no published Tamil pronunciation key for foreign words, and that is a citable negative rather than a gap in the search** -- Tamil dictionaries of English (the Madras University *Tamil Lexicon* and its successors) romanise Tamil for an English reader, which is the opposite direction, and Tamil-script transcription of foreign names is a newsroom practice rather than a codified system. So this table borrows four things and states what it adapted. **The notation for the sounds Tamil has no letter for is the superscript-digit convention of Tamil-script Sanskrit printing**: `ப` pa, `ப²` pha, `ப³` ba, `ப⁴` bha, over the five stop series. en.wikipedia's *Tamil script* records both the subscript form used in Sanskrit-Tamil books ('two, three, and four which stand for the unvoiced aspirated, voiced, voiced aspirated respectively') and that 'The Unicode Standard uses superscripted digits for the same purpose, as in ப² pha, ப³ ba, and ப⁴ bha', citing the Unicode Consortium; the superscript form is taken because it is the Standard's own and because `²` and `³` are Latin-1 while the subscripts are not. Both shipped faces confirm it independently: Noto Sans Tamil and Noto Serif Tamil carry exactly `² ³ ⁴` and `₂ ₃ ₄` out of the whole of Latin-1's superscripts and the Superscripts and Subscripts block, six codepoints that are precisely the two forms of this notation and nothing else. **The letters for the sounds Tamil does have are Modern Tamil's own**, including the five Grantha consonants `ஜ ஷ ஸ ஹ ஶ` the standard admits for non-Tamil sounds and `ஃப` for /f/, so the digit appears only where the alphabet really has a hole -- which is the Hindi nuqta decision one language later. **The abugida slot logic is `hi__hi-IN.json`'s**, three spellings per consonant chosen by position, and so is the C+`ய` device for a palatal, which hi.wikipedia's IPA tables use for /ɲ/ and /ʎ/. **The retroflex-for-English convention is Tamil's own and universal**: டிக்கெட், டாக்டர், வாட்டர், ஸ்டேஷன், in the `targets` block. `policy.reader_onsets` is Tamil's own division, which admits no onset cluster in a native word and the loanword clusters modern Tamil writes with a pulli -- ஸ்டேஷன், ப்ரெஞ்ச், பிளக், ஸ்ரீ.

deviations.rule: the published convention's own four-way index -- ச=ca, ச²=cha, ச³=ja, ச⁴=jha
deviations.why: Overruled for /dʒ/ and /z ʒ/, in opposite directions, and both times because a Tamil reader's own letters are better than a digit. /dʒ/ takes `ஜ`, an ordinary letter of Modern Tamil that this pack's own text uses (ஜனவரி, ஜூன், ஜான்), rather than the convention's `ச³`. And the digit is *extended* past the five stop series to the sibilants, which the published convention does not cover: /z/ is `ஸ³` and /ʒ/ is `ஷ³`. That is read as a feature -- ³ adds voice -- rather than as a fixed index, which is what makes the extension coherent, and it keeps /s/~/z/ and /ʃ/~/ʒ/ apart for English, French, Portuguese and Russian, which between them hold 3,046 voiced sibilants. The cost is that the reader has to be told the digits are features, which is what the legend says.

deviations.rule: native Tamil spelling, where `ச` is [s] word-initially and `ஸ` is a Grantha letter
deviations.why: Overruled: /s/ is `ஸ` and /tʃ/ is `ச`. Ordinary Tamil writes சரி [sari] and இறைச்சி [iraitʃːi] with the same letter, so `ச` is the one *ambiguous* consonant in the alphabet -- and a respelling column is the one place that cannot be afforded. `ஸ` is [s] in every position and every Tamil reader meets it in ஸ்டேஷன், பஸ், ஸ்ரீ.

deviations.rule: Tamil's positional voicing, under which an intervocalic `க` is read [ɡ]
deviations.why: **Suspended by declaration, and the legend is what declares it.** The superscript digits make this column a marked notation, and in a marked notation every letter is read at face value -- which is how a Tamil-script Sanskrit text works: once the digits are on the page the reader is out of Tamil sandhi and into one-letter-one-sound. The alternative was measured and rejected: writing an intervocalic voiceless stop as a geminate, which is Tamil's own device for it (ஹோட்டல், டிக்கெட், காப்பி), would collide with the **real** geminate contrast Italian, Japanese, Hindi and Arabic carry -- 243 `Cː` sequences in the corpus -- so /t/ and /tː/ would spell identically. The residual cost is named in `approximations`.

deviations.rule: A bare, unattached palatalisation mark ʲ (one with no consonant of its own to attach to) is dropped.
deviations.why: Romanian's espeak voice writes a genuinely doubled palatalisation on a word-final consonant before an asyllabic final -i (vorbiti "you speak" is vorbˈitsʲʲ) -- the first ʲ completes the tsʲ combination this table already has a rule for, and the second is left over with nothing to bind to. Every other reader table in this corpus already has exactly this fallback (`{"slot": "any", "ipa": "ʲ", "out": ""}`); this table had specific consonant+ʲ combinations but never needed the bare fallback until Romanian, the first source to double the mark, landed as a target. Added by the ro addition; see tmp/romanian.md.

approximations:
Sounds with no Tamil letter, and what they get. /ʔ ʕ/ are written as nothing, matching every South Asian script's treatment of hamza and ain. /ħ/ is ஹ and so is /ç/, where Hindi splits /ç/ by inventory -- Tamil ஹ is nearer to both the German ich-Laut and Japanese ひ than an aspirated velar would be. /x ɣ q qʰ/ are க² க³ க க², following Hindi's reasoning that a reader who does not make the uvular should not be told to. Every rhotic collapses onto ர -- /r ɾ ɹ ʁ ɽ ɽʰ/ -- because Tamil's own ற is a trill in careful speech and [tr] between vowels and no Tamil print writes a foreign r with it. /ʂ ɕ/ merge into ஷ with /ʃ/, and /ʐ ʑ/ into ஷ³ with /ʒ/. /y yː ø œ øː œː ɵ/ take the ஊ and ஒ/ஓ series: the front rounded quality is not writable at all, and Tamil print already spells München and Köln that way. /ɜ ɜː/ take the short அ, which is what நர்ஸ் and பர்ட் already write. Vietnamese's glottalised codas and its /ˀ/ are dropped with the tone. Korean's /ɰ/ shares the /w/ device and Mandarin's /ɥ/ the /j/ one.

**Three costs are sharper and are named rather than hidden.** *The dental/alveolar pair is not spelt.* /t/ and /t̪/ both take த and /n/ takes ந or ன by Tamil's own positional rule rather than by the phoneme, so Arabic's and Vietnamese's dental series prints as Tamil's own. *An unmarked stop between vowels is a gamble on the legend.* Tamil's reading rule voices it, and this column asks the reader not to -- so a reader who has not read the legend will say [waːɖar] for வாடர். The `targets` block removes the sharpest case by giving English and German the retroflex series, which Tamil already reads as a foreign spelling, but the general case is a real risk and the honest statement of it is that the legend is load-bearing rather than decorative. *And the digits are three more shapes to decode.* `tmp/ta/calibrate.py` measured that they never become the least distinguishable pair in the set at any print size, so they are legible; whether an ordinary Tamil reader who has not met Sanskrit-in-Tamil printing accepts them is a reviewer question and is the first thing to ask about this table.
note:
**Tamil is an abugida with no voiced or aspirated letter, so this table has two design decisions rather than one.** The first is where the pulli goes, and it is Hindi's: a consonant letter with nothing after it already says [a], so a cluster that forgets its pulli prints a vowel the target does not have. Every consonant therefore has three spellings and `spellSlot`'s position decides -- bare when it is the first thing in the syllable (`after_out: ""`) so a vowel sign can bind to it, pulli-then-letter anywhere else in an onset, and letter-then-pulli in a coda. Unlike Hindi's table, a **final** pulli is kept: Tamil writes வணக்கம், நான், பால் with it and dropping it would print a word Tamil does not have.

The second is the superscript digit, and the thing to know about it is that its **position is fixed by a fixup rather than by the letter map**. `ெ ே ை` are pre-base vowel signs, drawn to the left of the consonant they belong to, so `ப` + `²` + `ெ` would hand the shaper a sign with a Latin superscript to attach to and print a dotted circle. The phoneme rules emit the digit immediately after its base letter, one fixup swaps it past a following vowel sign, and the coda and medial-onset rules place it after the pulli themselves -- so no syllable can need the swap twice, which matters because a `syllable_fixups` regex is not global and replaces only its first match.

**Tamil writes vowel length, so `policy.length` is `none` and the vowels carry it themselves.** All five short/long pairs have letters -- அ/ஆ, இ/ஈ, உ/ஊ, எ/ஏ, ஒ/ஓ -- which is the one place this table is better off than Bengali's and Hindi's, both of which record the length collapse as a cost. Twelve vowel qualities are writable including the two diphthong signs ஐ and ஔ.

**No stress device, and all four were checked rather than assumed.** `caps` is dead on a caseless script. `acute` and `grave` are byte-identical no-ops, because `VOWEL_LETTERS` and `ACCENTED` in core/respell.js list Latin, Cyrillic and Greek vowels and no Tamil codepoint -- the wall Hebrew and Persian hit. `prime` U+02B9 would work, and Hindi's `’` fixup shows how to place one, but it is refused here for the reason the digits exist: this column already asks a Tamil reader to decode a notation, and the notation carries information the script cannot otherwise write while a stress mark carries information Tamil itself does not use -- Tamil stress is not contrastive (see `STRESS["ta"]` in scripts/build_ipa.py). Bengali and Urdu reached the same answer.
legend: ² = மூச்சுக் காற்று, ³ = ஒலிப்பு, ⁴ = இரண்டும். எழுத்தை உள்ளபடியே படியுங்கள்; - அசைப் பிரிவு.
